title: Remove Duplicate Letters
description: Brute force to optimized: generating every valid subsequence versus a monotonic stack guided by last-occurrence indices.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a string s, remove duplicate letters so that every letter appears exactly once, and the result is the LEXICOGRAPHICALLY SMALLEST possible among all such results, while preserving the relative order of the remaining letters from the original string.

blocks.text: Building the result greedily from left to right, a "larger" letter already placed can be safely REMOVED (and re-added later) if it still occurs again further along in the string; if it does not occur again, it must be kept now, since this is the only chance to include it.

blocks.title: Analogy: Building the Smallest Possible Word Using Every Letter Exactly Once
blocks.text: Picture assembling the smallest possible word from a longer string, using each distinct letter exactly once and preserving their relative order. If a letter placed so far is bigger than the current letter AND it appears again later, it is safe to remove it now (you can add it back when it appears again), always making the earliest possible position as small as possible.

blocks.caption: A monotonic stack pops a larger, already-placed letter only if it still appears again later in the string

blocks.text: Result: "abc". Starting "b","c" get pushed; then "a" arrives, popping "c" (reappears later) and "b" (reappears later), giving "a"; then "b","c" are re-added, giving "abc".

Before generating every valid subsequence using each letter once, notice that a greedy, monotonic-stack-based construction, informed by each letter's LAST occurrence, directly builds the lexicographically smallest valid result in a single pass.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Processing s left to right, if the current letter is already in the result (stack), it must be skipped, since each letter can appear only once in the final answer.

Observation 2: If the top of the stack (the most recently placed letter) is LARGER than the current letter, AND that top letter still occurs again later in the string, it is safe to POP it now, since it can be re-added at its later occurrence, and removing it now makes the result smaller.

Observation 3: If the top letter does NOT occur again later, it must be KEPT, since this is the only remaining chance to include it in the result.

Observation 4: Precomputing the LAST occurrence index of every letter (in one initial pass) lets this "does it occur again later" check be answered in O(1) at each step.

This leads to precomputing last occurrence indices, then a monotonic stack: for each letter (skipping already-used ones), pop any larger, already-placed letter from the stack as long as it reappears later, then push the current letter.
Generate every valid subsequence of s that uses each distinct letter exactly once, preserving relative order, and keep the lexicographically smallest one found.

items: Identify the set of distinct letters in s.
Generate every possible subsequence of s that includes each distinct letter exactly once, preserving their original relative order.
Compare all such subsequences lexicographically, keeping the smallest.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Generating every valid subsequence directly explores every possibility, guaranteed correct.
This costs exponential time in the worst case, far too slow for s up to 10^4 characters.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: exponential in the worst case.
Space: O(n) recursion depth.
Limitation: a monotonic-stack greedy approach, using precomputed last-occurrence indices, builds the answer directly in a single pass, achieving O(n) instead of exponential search.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why generating every subsequence is unnecessary: a greedy, local decision at each character (pop a larger already-placed letter if it is safe to re-add later, otherwise keep it) directly builds the globally optimal result.

Precomputing last occurrences: knowing the last index of every letter in O(n) upfront lets the "does this letter reappear later" check happen in O(1) at each step.

The monotonic stack construction: process s left to right; skip letters already in the result; otherwise, pop any larger letter at the top of the stack as long as it still reappears later, then push the current letter.

The core idea: a monotonic stack, guided by last-occurrence information, replaces exponential subsequence generation with a single O(n) pass.

Precompute last occurrence indices. Process s left to right with a stack and a "currently in result" set: skip already-used letters; pop larger, still-reappearing letters from the stack; push the current letter and mark it used.

blocks.caption: A monotonic stack, guided by last-occurrence indices, builds the smallest valid result in one pass

blocks.text: The monotonic stack maintains the smallest valid prefix possible at every step: a larger, already-placed letter is popped only when doing so is SAFE (it reappears later, so it can still be included in the final answer), which strictly improves the result by allowing a smaller letter to take an earlier position. If the larger letter does not reappear, popping it would lose it entirely, so it is correctly kept. This greedy, informed-by-last-occurrence process provably constructs the lexicographically smallest valid result.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), since each character is pushed and popped from the stack at most once.
Space: O(1) extra (bounded by the alphabet size, 26 for lowercase letters).

blocks.text: Remove Duplicate Letters is a strong example of a monotonic stack guided by "future occurrence" information, popping greedily only when doing so is provably safe (the popped element can still be re-added later).

Popping a larger letter even when it does NOT reappear later, permanently losing it from the result.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "lexicographically smallest result using each element exactly once, order preserved", think: a monotonic stack, popping only when the popped element reappears later.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Generating every valid subsequence costs exponential time; the monotonic stack with last-occurrence information costs O(n) time and O(1) extra space, the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: a monotonic stack, popping a larger already-placed element only when it is safe (it reappears later).
Core Idea: precompute last occurrence indices; process left to right, popping larger reappearing letters, skipping already-used ones, and pushing the current letter.
Time: exponential for generating every subsequence, O(n) for the optimized monotonic stack.
Space: O(n) recursion depth versus O(1) extra (bounded by alphabet size).
Most Important Observation: popping a larger letter is only safe if it reappears later; otherwise it must be kept now.
Interview Difficulty: a well-known, moderately hard monotonic stack problem.
One line memory trick: pop a larger, already-placed letter only if it reappears later.
